body.statement: Derive a necessary-and-sufficient inequality in \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,d\), including its boundary logarithms, for \(\rho_n^*\asymp\rho_{n,e}^*\). On its complement, characterize the order of \(\rho_n^*/\rho_{n,e}^*\) from the matched deterministic optimizations delivered by oeq:complete-frontier, and exhibit legal sequences in the unchanged class that certify strict divergence.
body.justification: The value of knowing assignment is a derived experiment-comparison frontier, not a generic first-order product-rate slogan.
body.gap: Hahn1998 establishes ATE ancillarity and KennedyBalakrishnanRobinsWasserman2024 establishes an estimation elbow, but neither compares these two homogeneity-testing experiments.
body.consumer: Study designers can determine when recording or externally supplying assignment probabilities changes the detectable scale of effect variation.

obligation.what_is_open: A necessary-and-sufficient equality region, its boundary logarithms, and the rate of divergence on the complementary parameter regimes.
obligation.obstruction: The supplied testing optimization has an unavoidable first-projection floor that is strictly slower than the proved critical radius in a legal no-penalty regime, and the supplied mixture optimization admits a tau-only tuple whose claimed lower scale contradicts the same upper bound. Thus neither frozen optimization can support the requested necessity argument or strict-divergence sequences.
obligation.attempted: The dense no-penalty comparison was proved directly, and both deterministic optimizations were stress-tested at dimension one, CATE smoothness one, propensity smoothness one tenth, and baseline smoothness nine tenths. Those checks yield the two negative theorems in this dispatch.
obligation.partial_result:
The proved comparison supplies the sufficient region
\[
 \alpha+\beta\ge\gamma\quad\text{and}\quad d\le4\gamma
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \rho_n^*\asymp\rho_{n,e}^*\asymp n^{-2\gamma/(4\gamma+d)}.
\]
At the boundary \(d=4\gamma\), this argument gives \(n^{-1/4}\) without a logarithm. Necessity and the order of the ratio on the complement are not established.
